Threat.value: Unexpected movement nearby causes me to react as if I am in danger
I watch other people closely for signs that they might harm me
Being superalert or watchful or on guard

Memory.value: I feel like I am only remembering parts of what happened and the rest is missing
When I try to explain what happened I lose the thread and cannot finish
I cannot tell a clear story of what happened even to myself

Negative Appraisals.value: The people or institutions that should have protected me let me down
The people responsible have faced no consequences

issues.item: Door and Lock Checking: I repeatedly check that doors and windows are locked
issues.explanation: This threat item is hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile. For a witnessed-other-trauma presentation, the other threat items describe hypervigilance and startle around other people, and the triggers/memory/appraisal items do not suggest a home-intrusion or boundary-violation danger theme. Repeated door/window checking points to a specific safety behavior focused on securing the environment, which is not supported elsewhere in the selected items and does not fit the formulation well, especially given that maladaptive-strategy links are inactive.

vignette: Kane, a 71‑year‑old man of Polynesian descent, has spent most of his adult life tending the till at the local grocery store in a small coastal town. Married to his wife of thirty‑five years, he enjoys the rhythm of his routine: early‑morning coffee, a steady stream of customers, the predictable opening and closing of the shop’s doors. Yet his days have become punctuated by the clatter of his own anxieties. One rainy Tuesday, as the afternoon rush pressed against the automatic doors, a confrontation erupted on the front sidewalk. A teenage boy had been shoved by a disgruntled customer, and in the ensuing scuffle a younger boy with a stroller – the toddler’s cry cutting through the din – was pushed off the curb. The older boy’s mother screamed, and a shop assistant tried to intervene. The scene was chaotic: the slamming of the back door as staff hurried to lock the store, the shrill wail of the infant, the sharp gasp of a passerby. Kane watched from the counter, helpless, as the boy’s mother fell to her knees, clutching the stroller with shaking hands. The chaos, the cries, the abrupt slamming door – it all imprinted itself on Kane’s memory in fragments that would haunt him for years. In the weeks that followed, the sounds that once were part of the grocery’s everyday soundtrack began to pull him into a state of hypervigilance. When a baby’s cry rang out near the snack aisle, he felt his heart leap, his eyes darting toward every corner as if unseen movement might strike. The sudden slam of a closing back door would send his pulse racing, as if danger lurked behind the threshold. These auditory triggers pulled him into a sense of threat, a feeling that the world was suddenly a place where a sudden movement could harm him. The triggers also sharpened his belief that the institutions that were supposed to protect him had betrayed him. The sound of a baby’s cry, the sharp slam of a door – each seemed to underscore the failure of the store’s security measures and the lack of response from the police who had passed by that afternoon. These associations fed into his negative appraisal that the world was indifferent and that the authorities had let him down. The emotional numbness that settled over him after the event was not simply a byproduct of stress; it became a lens that made every flash of memory feel incomplete. When he tried to explain what had happened, he would find himself staring at the space between the first crack of the door and the last word of the mother’s scream. He could not finish the story; it felt as if vital pieces were missing. This incomplete picture, in turn, reinforced his sense of institutional failure, because he could not piece together the events to see how the system had protected—or failed to protect—him. The gaps in his recollection also made the triggers more vivid. Each time he heard a baby’s cry, the memory of the missing details surged, turning the sound into a doorway to the trauma. The memory’s incompleteness, the negative appraisal of failure, and the triggers created a self‑reinforcing loop that amplified his threat perception. Kane’s heightened sense of danger fed back into his negative appraisal. Every time he felt a sudden startle from a movement near the register or a door slamming, he was reminded that safety had collapsed. That sense of threat hardened his conviction that institutions had no accountability; the same fear that kept him on guard also convinced him that no one would ever face consequences for their negligence. In this way, the threat reinforced his negative beliefs, while those beliefs pushed him into a state of hypervigilance, and the hypervigilance made the memories of the event more salient. The more he watched others closely for signs that they might harm him, the more he felt that the world was hostile and that he needed to stay on edge. His avoidance was not a conscious decision; it grew organically from the way each component fed into the next. Years of living with this cycle have taken a toll. Kane now skips the early morning shift, fearing the sudden slam of the door and the shrill cry that might erupt in the aisles. He keeps his conversations brief with his wife, worried that his stories of incompleteness and numbness will only deepen her concern. The store’s frequent rearrangements of shelves now trigger a startle that rattles his thoughts into the past, and each reminder of the failed protection of the authorities fuels a bitter conviction that justice was never served. The memory of the afternoon’s violence remains a jagged fragment, and the sense that the world was untrustworthy has become a constant backdrop to his everyday life. The day he finally called for help was after a child’s cry in the pharmacy aisle had him reaching for his hand, heart pounding, and a sense of imminent danger so acute that he could no longer focus on the task at hand. He feared that if he stayed in this relentless loop, his relationships and his work would unravel entirely. He was most afraid of being trapped in the unending cycle of threat and negative belief, yet he hoped that an outside perspective might untangle the connections that bound him so tightly to the past.
